title: Week 1: Getting Set Up
text:
Key Concepts

A website needs files, usually HTML, and a server that makes those files available online.
Quarto converts .qmd source files into .html pages.
Saving a source file, rendering a site, committing a snapshot, and pushing to GitHub are separate actions.
A .qmd file can combine YAML metadata, Markdown writing, executable R code, and rendered results.
Source files are edited by people; output and cache files are generated by tools.

This week helped me understand that building a reproducible website is a sequence rather than a single save button. I want to become more confident using R, Quarto, Git, and GitHub to create clear public-facing work. The number of separate steps still feels unfamiliar, but repeating the workflow should make it more natural.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
We reviewed the portfolio workflow, took a quiz, and began working with two core tools for public-policy data analysis:

dplyr, an R package for transforming tables.
tidycensus, an R package for downloading Census and American Community Survey (ACS) data.

The class connected data manipulation with an important data source: Census geography and ACS estimates.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
We reviewed the portfolio workflow, took a quiz, and began working with two core tools for public-policy data analysis:

dplyr, an R package for transforming tables.
tidycensus, an R package for downloading Census and American Community Survey (ACS) data.

The class connected data manipulation with an important data source: Census geography and ACS estimates.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
Key Concepts

An object stores a value or a table in R.
A function takes an input, performs an operation, and returns an output.
A tibble is a modern data frame: observations are rows and variables are columns.
dplyr verbs make table operations readable: filter rows, select columns, create variables, sort rows, and summarize groups.
The Decennial Census is a full population count every ten years; the ACS is a continuous sample survey that publishes estimates with margins of error.
A GEOID is a geographic identifier and should be stored as text so leading zeros are preserved.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
Reflection
This week clarified how R transforms tables with dplyr and how ACS data combine estimates with measures of uncertainty. I also learned that Census geography and GEOIDs must be understood before analysis begins. The most important habit is to treat an ACS estimate and its margin of error as a pair rather than focusing only on the estimate.

text:
Questions I Still Have

How should I compare two estimates when both have margins of error?
When should I choose long data rather than wide data for a real project?
How small can the geography become before ACS estimates are too uncertain for a policy decision?

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be.
Most people ignore it. In this assignment, you won’t.
In this analysis, I look at the number with a bachelor’s degree across counties in New York State, and ask which communities we measure most and least reliably.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Choosing what to measure

my_state <- "NY"        # two-letter abbreviation, in quotes
my_variable <- "B15003_022"     # the variable code, in quotes

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Pulling the data

county_data <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = my_variable,
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5"
)

Let’s look at what came back.

dim(county_data)

[1] 62  5

head(county_data)

# A tibble: 6 × 5
  GEOID NAME                         variable   estimate   moe
  <chr> <chr>                        <chr>         <dbl> <dbl>
1 36001 Albany County, New York      B15003_022    49653  1534
2 36003 Allegany County, New York    B15003_022     3787   306
3 36005 Bronx County, New York       B15003_022   130281  3296
4 36007 Broome County, New York      B15003_022    21526  1008
5 36009 Cattaraugus County, New York B15003_022     6055   387
6 36011 Cayuga County, New York      B15003_022     7436   457


The dataset contains 62 rows, one for each county in New York State, which matches the state’s 62 counties.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: How big is the margin of error?
text:
How big is the margin of error?
A margin of error of 3,000 means something very different for an estimate of 20,000 than for an estimate of 200,000. To compare across places, we need it as a percentage.

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100)

Now sort to see which counties are measured least reliably.

county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct) %>%
  head(10)

# A tibble: 10 × 4
   NAME                        estimate   moe moe_pct
   <chr>                          <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>
 1 Hamilton County, New York        586    99   16.9 
 2 Schuyler County, New York       1570   206   13.1 
 3 Yates County, New York          2427   269   11.1 
 4 Essex County, New York          4885   541   11.1 
 5 Fulton County, New York         5111   541   10.6 
 6 Sullivan County, New York       9476   986   10.4 
 7 Montgomery County, New York     3888   400   10.3 
 8 Washington County, New York     5649   573   10.1 
 9 Chenango County, New York       3554   353    9.93
10 Lewis County, New York          2060   203    9.85


Hamilton County has the largest margin of error relative to its estimate. Its margin of error is approximately 16.9% of the estimated number of residents whose highest educational attainment is a bachelor’s degree, making it the least reliably measured county for this variable.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Sorting counties into reliability categories

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 10 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

count(county_data, reliability)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  reliability         n
  <chr>           <int>
1 High confidence    24
2 Low confidence      8
3 Moderate           30

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Of New York State’s 62 counties, 24 fall into the high-confidence category, 30 are classified as moderate, and 8 fall into the low-confidence category.
text: Of New York State’s 62 counties, 24 fall into the high-confidence category, 30 are classified as moderate, and 8 fall into the low-confidence category.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
text:
Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
To answer this we need population and our variable side by side, in the same row. That means a wide pull.

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  GEOID NAME                         myvarE myvarM    popE  popM
  <chr> <chr>                         <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>
1 36001 Albany County, New York       49653   1534  315374    NA
2 36003 Allegany County, New York      3787    306   47027    NA
3 36005 Bronx County, New York       130281   3296 1419250    NA
4 36007 Broome County, New York       21526   1008  197738    NA
5 36009 Cattaraugus County, New York   6055    387   76479    NA
6 36011 Cayuga County, New York        7436    457   75464    NA



county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 10 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

Now compare the average population of counties in each reliability category.

county_wide %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE)
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  reliability     n_counties avg_population
  <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence         24        730694.
2 Low confidence           8         40855.
3 Moderate                30         66961.


The 24 high-confidence counties have an average population of approximately 730,694, compared with 66,961 for the 30 moderate-confidence counties and 40,855 for the 8 low-confidence counties. This pattern suggests that more populous counties tend to have more reliable ACS estimates, while smaller counties tend to have larger margins of error relative to their estimates.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy
Among all the counties in New York State, Hamilton County has the least reliable estimate: 586 residents aged 25 or older were estimated to have a bachelor’s degree as their highest level of education, with a margin of error of 99, or 16.9% of the estimate. Schuyler County follows with a relative margin of error of 13.1%, while Yates and Essex Counties are both about 11.1%. Overall, eight counties fall into the low-confidence category.
This reflects how the American Community Survey (ACS) works. The ACS estimates population characteristics from a sample rather than counting every resident. Smaller counties contribute fewer sampled households and residents, so each response carries more weight and the estimates have greater uncertainty. In this analysis, low-confidence counties have an average population of 40,855, compared with 730,694 in high-confidence counties.
Ignoring this margin of error might lead to unfair policy decisions. If a state agency directed workforce-development funding toward counties with fewer bachelor’s degree holders, it might treat every county estimate as equally precise. If a small county’s bachelor’s degree count were overestimated, it could appear better educated and receive less support than it needs as the result. Rural counties such as Hamilton, Schuyler, and Yates are especially vulnerable because their limited sample sizes make their estimates less stable. Agencies should consider margins of error and avoid making funding decisions based on small differences alone.

section: Optional challenges - For those craving more
text:
Optional challenges - For those craving more
Challenge 4: To examine how geographic scale affects uncertainty, I repeated the analysis for census tracts within Onondaga County, New York, which includes the city of Syracuse.

tract_data <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  variables = my_variable,
  state = my_state,
  county = "Onondaga",
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5"
)

dim(tract_data)

[1] 142   5

head(tract_data)

# A tibble: 6 × 5
  GEOID       NAME                                       variable estimate   moe
  <chr>       <chr>                                      <chr>       <dbl> <dbl>
1 36067000100 Census Tract 1; Onondaga County; New York  B15003_…      383   137
2 36067000200 Census Tract 2; Onondaga County; New York  B15003_…      213   118
3 36067000300 Census Tract 3; Onondaga County; New York  B15003_…      177    64
4 36067000400 Census Tract 4; Onondaga County; New York  B15003_…      500   182
5 36067000501 Census Tract 5.01; Onondaga County; New Y… B15003_…      268   148
6 36067000600 Census Tract 6; Onondaga County; New York  B15003_…      214   128



tract_data <- tract_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100)

tract_data %>%
  summarize(
    n_tracts = n(),
    median_moe_pct = median(moe_pct),
    mean_moe_pct = mean(moe_pct),
    min_moe_pct = min(moe_pct),
    max_moe_pct = max(moe_pct)
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 5
  n_tracts median_moe_pct mean_moe_pct min_moe_pct max_moe_pct
     <int>          <dbl>        <dbl>       <dbl>       <dbl>
1      142           32.1         37.3        14.3        103.



county_data %>%
  filter(NAME == "Onondaga County, New York") %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct)

# A tibble: 1 × 4
  NAME                      estimate   moe moe_pct
  <chr>                        <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>
1 Onondaga County, New York    68569  2067    3.01


At the county level, Onondaga County has an estimated 68,569 residents aged 25 or older whose highest educational attainment is a bachelor’s degree, with a relative margin of error of approximately 3.0%. Across its 142 census tracts, however, the median relative margin of error is 32.1% and the mean is 37.3%, with values ranging from 14.3% to 103.1%. This comparison shows that ACS estimates become much less precise at smaller geographic scales because each tract is represented by a smaller sample.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
Notes

1. Objects, functions, arguments, and comments
This example keeps counties with populations above 50,000 and stores the result in a new object:
result <- filter(counties, population > 50000) # Keep larger counties

result is the object that stores the output.
<- is the assignment operator.
filter() is the function.
counties is the input data.
population > 50000 is an argument or condition.
Text after # is a comment and is not executed.

R is case-sensitive, so result and Result are different objects. Using lowercase object and function names consistently prevents avoidable errors.


2. Packages: install once, load each session
A package is a collection of functions. Installation happens once on a computer; loading happens at the start of each new R session.
# Run once on a computer
install.packages("dplyr")
install.packages("tidycensus")

# Run in each new R session
library(dplyr)
library(tidycensus)
I think of install.packages() as putting a book on the shelf and library() as taking that book off the shelf to use it.


3. Tibbles and dplyr verbs
A tibble is a table in which each row is an observation and each column is a variable.



NAME
INCOME
MOE




Adams
78,975
1,237


Berks
74,617
4,372


Bucks
104,200
2,374



Common dplyr verbs:

filter() keeps rows that meet a condition.
select() keeps or reorders columns.
mutate() adds or changes a computed column.
arrange() changes row order; desc() requests descending order.
group_by() and summarize() turn many rows into group-level summaries.

A correct mutate() expression must name the new column:
counties <- counties |>
  mutate(income_doubled = income * 2)
The same sequence of operations can be written step by step:
step_1 <- filter(counties, moe_pct > 10)
step_2 <- arrange(step_1, desc(moe_pct))
step_3 <- select(step_2, NAME, moe_pct)
Or as one pipeline. Both %>% and the base-R pipe |> mean roughly “and then.”
new_data <- counties |>
  filter(moe_pct > 10) |>
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) |>
  select(NAME, moe_pct)
Grouping allows us to calculate one value for each category:
county_income |>
  group_by(STATE) |>
  summarize(min_income = min(INCOME))


4. Decennial Census and the ACS
The two Census Bureau products answer different questions:








Product
What it provides
Important limitation




Decennial Census
A full population count every 10 years, down to Census blocks
Limited social and economic characteristics


American Community Survey
Ongoing sample-based estimates for income, education, housing, commuting, and more
Every estimate includes uncertainty



Important ACS products:

ACS 1-year: more current, but available only for areas with populations of 65,000 or more.
ACS 5-year: combines five years of responses, covers small geographies, and is generally more precise for tract or block-group analysis.
ACS 3-year: discontinued after the 2013 release.

For ACS data, always keep two values in mind:
Estimate (E)        the estimated value
Margin of Error (M) the uncertainty around that estimate


5. Census geography and GEOIDs
The basic geographic hierarchy is:
state -> county -> Census tract -> block group -> Census block
Census tract boundaries can change over time. Block groups are available in ACS 5-year data, but their smaller samples often produce large margins of error, so they should be used cautiously rather than rejected automatically. Census blocks are primarily associated with Decennial Census data.
A tract GEOID has 11 digits. For example:
42101000100
42     = Pennsylvania state FIPS
101    = Philadelphia County FIPS
000100 = Census tract code
GEOIDs are identifiers, not quantities, so they should be stored as character strings:
geoid <- "42101000100"


6. ACS variable codes and tidycensus
In the raw ACS name B19013_001E:

B19013 is the table number.
001 is the line number.
E means estimate; M means margin of error.

When using tidycensus, the variable is normally requested without the final E or M:
library(tidycensus)

county_data <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(
    median_income = "B19013_001",
    total_population = "B01003_001"
  ),
  state = "PA",
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)


7. Long and wide data

Long (tidy) output: one geography-variable combination per row, with variable, estimate, and moe columns.
Wide output: one geographic unit per row, with separate estimate and MOE columns such as median_incomeE and median_incomeM.

Long format is useful for repeated operations across variables; wide format is often convenient for comparison, modeling, and joins.

title: Week 1: Getting Set Up
text:
Notes

1. What is a website?
In the class workflow, a website has two main parts:
a folder of HTML files + a server that is always online
For this portfolio:
Quarto creates the HTML files
GitHub Pages hosts those files online
The complete path from source to website is:
.qmd source file -> Quarto Render -> .html page -> GitHub Pages
I normally edit the .qmd source rather than the generated .html file.


2. Quarto and Render
Quarto is a publishing system that combines writing, code, and results in one document. It can render a .qmd file as a webpage, PDF, slide deck, or Word document.
When I select Render, Quarto:

Reads the .qmd file from top to bottom.
Finds executable code chunks.
Sends R code to R and receives the results.
Combines the writing, code, and output into HTML.

Saving only records edits in the source file. Rendering rebuilds the output page, so Save is not Render.


3. Anatomy of a .qmd file
A Quarto document normally contains three parts:
YAML header + Markdown text + R code chunks

YAML header
The YAML header goes at the very top and stores page metadata:
---
title: "Week 1: Getting Set Up"
description: "My first weekly note"
date: 2026-08-28
---
Important YAML rules:

The opening and closing --- lines matter.
A colon must be followed by a space.
Dates should use YYYY-MM-DD.
Use plain quotation marks.



Markdown
Markdown provides headings, paragraphs, lists, emphasis, and links:
## What I Learned

This is a paragraph with a [link](https://quarto.org/).

- First point
- Second point


R code chunks
An executable R chunk in a Quarto file uses an opening fence labeled {r}. The code inside a chunk might look like this:
library(tidycensus)

x <- 2 + 2
print(x)
R code should be placed inside a code chunk when I want Quarto to run it and include the result in the page.



4. Files and folders
A useful question is: Who is this file for?
Files I edit directly:
index.qmd
about.qmd
weekly-notes/*.qmd
assignments/*.qmd
_quarto.yml
Files and folders mainly used by software:







Item
Purpose




.Rproj
Opens the folder as an RStudio project


.gitignore
Tells Git which files not to track


.Renviron
Stores environment variables and secrets such as API keys


docs/
Contains the rendered website published by GitHub Pages


_freeze/
Stores Quarto execution results and cache data



The key rule is: edit source files and allow Quarto to regenerate output files.


5. Why index.qmd matters
Web servers normally look for index.html when a visitor requests a folder URL. Quarto creates that file from index.qmd:
index.qmd -> Render -> docs/index.html
That is why the portfolio homepage source file is named index.qmd.


6. Git, GitHub.com, and GitHub Desktop
These tools are related but have different roles:

Git is the version-control system running locally on my computer.
GitHub.com stores an online copy of the repository.
GitHub Desktop provides buttons and menus that send commands to Git.

Commit and push are also different:
Commit = save a labeled snapshot in the local Git repository
Push   = send local commits to GitHub.com


7. The portfolio workflow
Edit -> Save -> Render -> Commit -> Push -> wait -> refresh the live site
Each step changes a different version of the work:

Edit and Save: update the local source file.
Render: rebuild the local website output.
Commit: record a labeled local snapshot.
Push: transfer commits to GitHub.com.
Refresh: check the published GitHub Pages site.



8. Markdown, R scripts, and Quarto documents
Markdown text = writing and formatting, without calculation
R script      = reusable code
.qmd document = writing + code + results
An R script is useful for experimenting with code and building reusable analysis. A .qmd document is useful when I need to explain the analysis and publish its results together.

title: Verify the Claim: Poverty Change in Philadelphia
text:
Part 2: Test

Poverty rates and margins of error
The ACS publishes 90% margins of error (MOEs) for the counts. Because a poverty rate is a proportion, I calculate its MOE with moe_prop() rather than reusing the MOE for the numerator.


Show code
poverty_2010 <- poverty_2010 %>%
  mutate(
    poverty_rate = below_povertyE / totalE,
    poverty_rate_moe = moe_prop(
      num = below_povertyE,
      denom = totalE,
      moe_num = below_povertyM,
      moe_denom = totalM
    )
  )

poverty_2017 <- poverty_2017 %>%
  mutate(
    poverty_rate = below_povertyE / totalE,
    poverty_rate_moe = moe_prop(
      num = below_povertyE,
      denom = totalE,
      moe_num = below_povertyM,
      moe_denom = totalM
    )
  )




Missing values


Show code
missing_2010 <- poverty_2010 %>%
  filter(
    totalE == 0 |
      is.na(poverty_rate) |
      is.na(poverty_rate_moe)
  )

missing_2017 <- poverty_2017 %>%
  filter(
    totalE == 0 |
      is.na(poverty_rate) |
      is.na(poverty_rate_moe)
  )

nrow(missing_2010)


[1] 7


Show code
nrow(missing_2017)


[1] 8


Seven tracts in 2006–2010 and eight in 2013–2017 have a denominator of zero and therefore an undefined poverty rate. These tracts have no estimated population in the poverty universe, so I exclude them rather than treating an undefined rate as zero. After the two periods are matched, 376 tracts have usable estimates in both periods.


Reliability
I convert each 90% MOE to a standard error by dividing by 1.645, then calculate the coefficient of variation (CV) as the standard error divided by the poverty-rate estimate. Following the required Jurjevich et al. (2018) thresholds, a CV below 12% is reliable, 12–40% is somewhat reliable, and above 40% is unreliable.


Show code
poverty_2010_valid <- poverty_2010 %>%
  filter(
    totalE > 0,
    !is.na(poverty_rate),
    !is.na(poverty_rate_moe)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    period = "2006–2010",
    poverty_rate_se = poverty_rate_moe / 1.645,
    cv = poverty_rate_se / poverty_rate * 100,
    reliability = case_when(
      cv < 12  ~ "Reliable",
      cv <= 40 ~ "Somewhat reliable",
      TRUE     ~ "Unreliable"
    )
  )

poverty_2017_valid <- poverty_2017 %>%
  filter(
    totalE > 0,
    !is.na(poverty_rate),
    !is.na(poverty_rate_moe)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    period = "2013–2017",
    poverty_rate_se = poverty_rate_moe / 1.645,
    cv = poverty_rate_se / poverty_rate * 100,
    reliability = case_when(
      cv < 12  ~ "Reliable",
      cv <= 40 ~ "Somewhat reliable",
      TRUE     ~ "Unreliable"
    )
  )

reliability_counts <- bind_rows(
  poverty_2010_valid,
  poverty_2017_valid
) %>%
  count(period, reliability)




Show code
poverty_2017_valid %>%
  mutate(
    dot = case_when(
      cv < 12  ~ "🟢",
      cv <= 40 ~ "🟡",
      TRUE     ~ "🔴"
    ),
    flag = reliability,
    NAME = str_remove(NAME, ", Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania"),
    rate = poverty_rate * 100,
    rate_moe = poverty_rate_moe * 100
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(cv)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 15) %>%
  select(dot, NAME, rate, rate_moe, cv, flag) %>%
  gt() %>%
  fmt_number(columns = c(rate, rate_moe), decimals = 1) %>%
  fmt_number(columns = cv, decimals = 1) %>%
  cols_label(
    dot = "",
    NAME = "Census tract",
    rate = "Poverty rate (%)",
    rate_moe = "MOE (percentage points)",
    cv = "CV (%)",
    flag = "Reliability"
  ) %>%
  cols_align(align = "center", columns = dot) %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Fifteen least reliable tract poverty-rate estimates",
    subtitle = "Philadelphia County, 2013–2017 ACS five-year estimates"
  ) %>%
  tab_source_note(

Reliability is uneven. In 2006–2010, 11 tracts are reliable, 321 somewhat reliable, and 45 unreliable. In 2013–2017, the corresponding counts are 22, 332, and 22. The table displays the least reliable recent estimates rather than hiding them; these large CVs are a reason to test uncertainty explicitly before interpreting apparent change.


Change between periods


Show code
poverty_wide <- bind_rows(
  poverty_2010_valid,
  poverty_2017_valid
) %>%
  select(GEOID, NAME, period, poverty_rate, poverty_rate_moe) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = period,
    values_from = c(poverty_rate, poverty_rate_moe)
  )

poverty_tested <- poverty_wide %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(`poverty_rate_2006–2010`),
    !is.na(`poverty_rate_2013–2017`)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    change = `poverty_rate_2013–2017` - `poverty_rate_2006–2010`,
    se_1 = `poverty_rate_moe_2006–2010` / 1.645,
    se_2 = `poverty_rate_moe_2013–2017` / 1.645,
    se_diff = sqrt(se_1^2 + se_2^2),
    moe_diff = se_diff * 1.645,
    z = change / se_diff,
    significant = abs(z) > 1.645,
    result = case_when(
      significant & change > 0 ~ "Significant increase",
      significant & change < 0 ~ "Significant decrease",
      TRUE ~ "Not statistically detectable"
    )
  )

change_counts <- poverty_tested %>%
  count(result)




Show code
ggplot(change_counts, aes(x = result, y = n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Results of the tract-level change test",
    subtitle = "Individual 90% tests for 376 matched Philadelphia census tracts",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Number of tracts",
    caption = "Source: U.S. Census Bureau, ACS five-year estimates."
  )





Most Philadelphia tracts did not have a statistically detectable change in poverty rate.






Error-bar visualization
For readability, the figure below shows the 20 largest absolute changes among tracts whose changes are statistically detectable. The complete significance count above still includes all 376 matched tracts.


Show code
change_plot_data <- poverty_tested %>%
  filter(significant) %>%
  arrange(desc(abs(change))) %>%
  slice_head(n = 20) %>%
  mutate(
    NAME = str_remove(NAME, ", Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania"),
    change_pp = change * 100,
    moe_diff_pp = moe_diff * 100,
    direction = case_when(
      change > 0 ~ "Increase",
      TRUE ~ "Decrease"
    )
  )

change_plot_data %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(NAME, change_pp), y = change_pp)) +
  geom_col(aes(fill = direction)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = change_pp - moe_diff_pp,
                    ymax = change_pp + moe_diff_pp), width = 0.3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Largest statistically detectable changes in poverty rate",
    subtitle = "Twenty largest absolute tract changes, 2006–2010 vs. 2013–2017",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Change in poverty rate (percentage points)",
    fill = NULL,
    caption = "Error bars show 90% margins of error; dashed line marks no change. Source: U.S. Census Bureau ACS."
  )





Largest statistically detectable tract-level changes in poverty rates, with 90% margins of error.




Of the 376 matched tracts, 36 show a statistically detectable increase, 27 show a detectable decrease, and 313 show no detectable change at 90% confidence. The evidence therefore supports uneven change across Philadelphia, but not a simple citywide story in which poverty clearly rose everywhere.

title: Verify the Claim: Poverty Change in Philadelphia
text:
Part 3: Adjudicate
Supported. The article’s broader claim that poverty increased sharply in some parts of Philadelphia is supported at the tract level. Thirty-six of 376 comparable tracts show statistically detectable increases. Not supported. The results do not support the impression that rising poverty was widespread across the city’s tracts. Most tracts—313 of 376—show no statistically detectable change, while 27 show a detectable decrease.
Cannot be determined. The exact claims for Fairhill (61%), Eastwick (12% to 26%), and Holmesburg’s white poverty rate (2% to 19%) cannot be reproduced from this tract analysis. The article does not disclose which tracts it aggregated into each informal neighborhood. The Holmesburg claim additionally requires race-specific poverty data, and the article’s explanations involving opioids, migration, or displacement would require evidence beyond these ACS estimates. Those claims are therefore not disproved; they remain unverified with the published methodological detail.

title: Verify the Claim: Poverty Change in Philadelphia
text:
Part 4: Rewrite

The American Community Survey shows that poverty changed unevenly across Philadelphia between 2006–2010 and 2013–2017. Among 376 census tracts with usable estimates in both periods, 36 had statistically detectable increases in poverty rates, 27 had detectable decreases, and 313 showed no detectable change at 90% confidence. These results support the conclusion that poverty worsened in some parts of the city, but not that the increase was widespread. The exact figures reported for Fairhill, Eastwick, and Holmesburg cannot be reproduced from tract data alone because the article did not publish which tracts were combined into each neighborhood. The Holmesburg claim about white poverty also requires race-specific poverty data.

text:
Part 1b: Join by what
How much has income changed since 2015? Pull the older estimates. No geometry is needed, because this is just a table.

income_15 <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  state = "PA",
  county = "Philadelphia",
  variables = c(med_inc_15 = "B19013_001"),
  year = 2015,
  output = "wide",

) %>%

nrow(income_15)

[1] 384

nrow(philly_tracts)

[1] 391


Stop and look: The row counts are different. Before you join, predict why.
Now join the 2015 table onto your tracts. The key is the column both tables share.

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  left_join(income_15, by = "GEOID")

nrow(philly_tracts)   # did the row count change?

philly_tracts %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%

    n_tracts = n(),

text:
Part 2: Bring in the stations
Indego publishes live station locations as GeoJSON. st_read() reads it directly from the URL.

stations <- st_read("https://www.rideindego.com/stations/json/", quiet = TRUE)

nrow(stations)

title: Week 4 Lab: Who Does Indego Reach?
text:
Part 3: Join by where
In Part 1b, the join failed because it matched on a label (GEOID), and the label changed. st_join() matches on location instead: a row is matched to whatever it sits on top of. Stations don’t have a GEOID column, and they don’t need one.
Every station gets its tract’s attributes:

stations_with_tract <- st_join(stations, philly_tracts)

stations_with_tract %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(name, GEOID, med_incE, reliability) %>%
  head()

                               name       GEOID med_incE reliability
1 Municipal Services Building Plaza 42101000403   187743    Moderate
2                 Welcome Park, NPS 42101001002   137250    Moderate
3                     40th & Spruce 42101008802    31293    Moderate
4            11th & Pine, Kahn Park 42101001101    61850    Moderate
5         Temple University Station 42101037700    22621    Moderate
6                     33rd & Market 42101009000    38976        High


Now go the other way and count stations per tract. The first route is the Week 2 collapse pattern:

station_counts <- stations_with_tract %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  count(GEOID)

The second route counts directly:

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  mutate(n_stations = lengths(st_intersects(., stations)))


Check your work

sum(philly_tracts$n_stations)

[1] 302

nrow(stations)

[1] 319


These probably don’t match. Discuss as a team: Why not? Find at least one station that explains the gap.
Hints: Look for stations where GEOID is NA in stations_with_tract. For double counts, look for stations that intersect more than one tract: which(lengths(st_intersects(stations, philly_tracts)) > 1).

title: Week 4 Lab: Who Does Indego Reach?
section: Part 4: How far is the nearest station?
text:
Part 4: How far is the nearest station?
st_distance() returns a matrix, not a column. Look at its shape first:

centroids <- st_centroid(st_geometry(philly_tracts))

dim(st_distance(centroids, stations))

[1] 391 319


Instead, find the nearest station for each tract, then measure only that one distance:

nearest_idx <- st_nearest_feature(centroids, stations)

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  mutate(
    dist_ft = as.numeric(
      st_distance(centroids, stations[nearest_idx, ], by_element = TRUE)
    ),
    dist_mi = dist_ft / 5280
  )

summary(philly_tracts$dist_mi)

    Min.  1st Qu.   Median     Mean  3rd Qu.     Max. 
 0.01893  0.15554  0.41382  1.84137  2.73916 10.93093

title: Week 4 Lab: Who Does Indego Reach?
section: Part 5: Buffers, filters, and cutting the dough
text:
Part 5: Buffers, filters, and cutting the dough
Build a half-mile zone around every station and merge the circles into one shape. Remember your units.

station_zone <- stations %>%
  st_buffer(dist = 0.5*5280) %>%
  st_union()

Pick whole cookies: which tracts don’t touch the zone at all?

outside_zone <- philly_tracts %>%
  st_filter(station_zone, .predicate = st_disjoint)

nrow(outside_zone)

[1] 162


Cut the dough: what share of each tract’s area falls inside the zone?

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  mutate(tract_area = as.numeric(st_area(.)))

covered <- philly_tracts %>%
  st_intersection(station_zone) %>%
  mutate(covered_area = as.numeric(st_area(.))) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(GEOID, covered_area)

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  left_join(covered, by = "GEOID") %>%
  mutate(pct_covered = replace_na(covered_area / tract_area, 0) * 100)

Notice: that last step is the left_join() from Part 1b. It’s a join by what (GEOID), used to bring a join-by-where result back into the table. The two kinds of join work together.

title: Week 4 Lab: Who Does Indego Reach?
text:
Part 6: The Challenge
You now have three different definitions of “has access”:

Distance: the tract centroid is within X miles of a station (dist_mi)
Touch: the tract touches the half-mile zone at all (st_filter)
Coverage: at least Y% of the tract’s area is inside the zone (pct_covered)


Your team’s task

Define “low-income.” For example, you could use the bottom quartile of tract median income, or a dollar threshold. Pick one and write it down.
Define “access.” Choose one of the three definitions above and set its threshold.
Answer the question. Which low-income tracts lack access? Produce:

The count of low-income tracts without access
A map showing them (a geom_sf() layer plus the stations)
The reliability breakdown: of those tracts, how many have High / Moderate / Low reliability income estimates?

Defend one decision in 2–3 sentences. Why this access definition and not another? How would your count change if you used a different one?

Scoring (for bragging rights, not grades)








Points




Count is correct for your stated definitions
2


Map shows the right tracts and the stations, with a title that states your definitions
2


Reliability breakdown included
1


Randomly chosen presenter explains the decision clearly
3


Team shows how the count changes under a second definition
+1





Before you present, discuss

If a tract is “low-income” with a CV of 45%, does it belong on your list? What would you tell Indego about it?
Your three access definitions give different counts. Which one would an Indego planner prefer? Which one would a neighborhood advocate prefer?

title: Week 4 Lab: Who Does Indego Reach?
text:
If you’re curious

Indego stations have a totalDocks property. Does “access” mean the same thing next to a 10-dock station and a 35-dock station?
Replace the centroid with st_point_on_surface(). Does any tract’s distance change a lot? Why might a centroid fall in an odd place for some tract shapes?
Straight-line distance ignores the Schuylkill, I-95, and rail yards. Which tracts do you suspect are farther in practice than your map shows?

title: Verify the Claim: Poverty Change in Philadelphia
text:
This report evaluates claims in Alfred Lubrano’s 2018 article, “New Census figures on Philly neighborhoods show inequality, high numbers of whites living in poverty”. The article describes Philadelphia’s 2013–2017 poverty rate as about 26% and reports large increases in several named neighborhoods relative to 2006–2010. Because the article does not publish its tract-to-neighborhood crosswalk, I use census tracts as the unit of analysis and test the broader claim that poverty increased across parts of Philadelphia. I do not attempt the optional neighborhood aggregation.
I use ACS detailed table B17001: B17001_001 is the total population for whom poverty status is determined (the denominator), and B17001_002 is the population below the poverty level (the numerator). I use the 2010 and 2017 ACS five-year releases because they correspond exactly to the article’s 2006–2010 and 2013–2017 periods and provide tract-level estimates. The periods do not overlap: 2006–2010 ends before 2013–2017 begins, with 2011–2012 between them. Treating the estimates as independent is therefore appropriate for the change test, but each value still describes a pooled five-year period rather than a single-year snapshot.


Show code
poverty_2010 <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  variables = c(
    total = "B17001_001",
    below_poverty = "B17001_002"
  ),
  state = "PA",
  county = "Philadelphia",
  year = 2010,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

poverty_2017 <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  variables = c(
    total = "B17001_001",
    below_poverty = "B17001_002"
  ),
  state = "PA",
  county = "Philadelphia",
  year = 2017,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)
